attribution.note: Zitron's own summary sentence in his post. He paraphrases the WSJ only for the $3bn figure, not for the three descriptions of the software.

semantics.note: A three-part present-tense description of OpenAI's software. Dropping 'only' from 'only loses money' slightly softens the wording but does not change what is tested.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: a 2024 loss, a measurable hallucination rate, and gains public before the post. 'No sign' is a strong negative, so any clear published sign of improvement counts against it. Where the bar for 'meaningful' sits is a judgment call, and it decides part three.

evidence.note: CNBC, Sept 2024: OpenAI expected about a $5bn loss on 2024 revenue. This is a press-reported projection, not audited, but it fits the contract's estimate basis. Supports 'loses money'.

OpenAI's own system card: GPT-4.5 still hallucinates on 19% of PersonQA, which supports 'still hallucinates'. The same table shows the rate falling from 0.30 (GPT-4o) and accuracy rising, which cuts against part three. Company disclosure.
OpenAI's launch post, four days before the post, claims fewer hallucinations and more reliability. This is the company describing itself, so it is weak alone, but e2's figures back it.

Independent ARC Prize result, Dec 2024: o3 preview scored 75.7% on ARC-AGI-1 against 5% for GPT-4o, called a step-function gain. Caveat: the tested model was tuned on ARC training data. Still a clear published sign of improvement.

reviews.rationale: Parts one and two hold: OpenAI was reported to expect about a $5bn 2024 loss (e1), and GPT-4.5 still hallucinated on 19% of PersonQA (e2). Part three fails: before the post there were published signs of meaningful gains, including an independent ARC-AGI jump for o3 (e4) and a lower hallucination rate with higher accuracy versus GPT-4o (e2, e3). The contract's support condition needs all three parts, so the claim is not supported as a whole.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: A necessity claim, so causal is the right kind. The drafter writes 'data center expansion' in general, while the nearest antecedent is Microsoft's expansion, which is how the contract reads it. Either reading gives an untested necessity claim with no measure or period.

contract.note: Grading it as an untestable counterfactual necessity claim is fair to his words. He gave no measure of 'evolving and expanding', and the situation the claim needs, expansion actually stalling, did not occur.

evidence.note: Microsoft's Q4 FY25 capital spending was $24.2bn. Its expansion did not stall, so there is no test case. Company disclosure.
Microsoft guided to Q1 FY26 capital spending above $30bn, which confirms continued expansion. Context only; it says nothing about whether expansion is necessary.

reviews.rationale: 'Absolutely necessary' is a counterfactual necessity claim with no stated measure or period. Testing it would need a period in which the expansion stalled, and the packet shows Microsoft kept increasing capital spending. The claim cannot be observed true or false.
